definition.text: A region with exceptionally high biodiversity, especially species found nowhere else, that is threatened by human activity.

facts.text: Norman Myers developed the concept in articles in 1988 and 1990, revised in 2000.
To qualify, a region must hold at least 1,500 endemic vascular plant species (over 0.5% of the world total) and have lost at least 70% of its primary vegetation.
Globally, 36 zones qualify.
Hotspots cover just 2.4% of the planet's surface yet support nearly 60% of the world's plant, bird, mammal, reptile and amphibian species.
Most hotspots are tropical, and only a small share of their land is protected.
Critics note that the hotspot approach ignores the cost of conservation and phylogenetic diversity.

definition.text: Systems that rank places for conservation by their species richness, endemism and threat, so limited funds go where they matter most.

facts.text: WWF's Global 200 Ecoregions picks priorities from 14 terrestrial, 3 freshwater and 4 marine habitat types, and every hotspot contains at least one.
BirdLife International has identified 218 Endemic Bird Areas and more than 11,000 Important Bird Areas.
The Alliance for Zero Extinction has identified 595 sites holding the most threatened endemic species.

definition.text: The process by which separate ecological communities become more and more alike over time.

facts.text: It can be genetic, taxonomic or functional, and it means a loss of beta diversity.
It stems mainly from extinctions of native species and invasions of non-native ones, and human pressure has accelerated it.
It need not lower local species richness; communities can gain species and still grow more similar.
In 201 Chilean watersheds compared over 200 years, about 65% of comparisons showed homogenization.
Ecologists worry that simpler, more similar ecosystems will be less resilient to stress.

definition.text: Meat from wild animals hunted for people to eat, especially in Africa.

facts.text: It is a main source of animal protein and income for poor rural communities in humid tropical forests.
As of 2016, 301 terrestrial mammal species were threatened with extinction by bushmeat hunting, including all pangolin species.
The trade in West and Central Africa was estimated at 1–5 million tonnes a year around the turn of the 21st century.
Hunting for one's own use in large landscapes can be sustainable, but market hunting threatens large, slow-breeding species.
The "bushmeat crisis", coined in 2007, names the double threat of vanishing food supplies and wildlife extinctions.
Logging roads and trucks give hunters access to remote forests and carry meat to towns.
Suggested remedies include affordable alternative protein, giving communities rights over wildlife, and enforcing protected areas.

definition.text: The link by which falling fish supplies push people to hunt more wild animals, because the two foods substitute for each other.

facts.text: In Ghana, depletion of fish stocks by foreign and local fleets led people to hunt animals in nature reserves instead.
Over 30 years of data tie sharp declines in 41 wildlife species to a falling fish supply.
A decline in one resource raises demand and price for the other.

definition.text: The jump of diseases from wild animals to people, made more likely by hunting, butchering and eating wildlife.

facts.text: HIV likely first passed to humans through contact with infected bushmeat.
Ebola outbreaks in the Congo Basin and Gabon in the 1990s were associated with butchering and eating chimpanzees and bonobos.
Deforestation, fragmentation and expanding human activity in wildlife habitat increase contact and so spillover.
The One Health framework treats human, animal and environmental health as interconnected.
